title: In re Schoenhals
description: Whether John H. Schoenhals' mandatory life without parole (LWOP) sentence for aggravated first degree murder, committed at age 20, is unconstitutional and whether his personal restraint petition is timely under the "significant change in the law" exemption.
plaintiff_argument: Schoenhals argues his LWOP sentence is unconstitutional based on Monschke and Carter, which require consideration of youth as a mitigating factor for 18-20 year olds, and that Monschke constitutes a "significant change in the law" making his petition timely.
defendant_argument: The State argues Schoenhals' petition is time-barred and that Monschke does not constitute a "significant change in the law" or that he has not shown actual and substantial prejudice.
decision_outcome: The court grants Schoenhals' personal restraint petition, finding his mandatory LWOP sentence unconstitutional, and remands the case for a new sentencing hearing.

title: In re the Detention of M.E. and R.S.
description: Whether the caseload limits in the Standards for Indigent Defense are mandatory and whether the trial court exceeded its authority in ordering the King County Department of Public Defense (DPD) to provide counsel in civil commitment cases despite DPD's capacity concerns.
plaintiff_argument: DPD argued that caseload limits are mandatory and the trial court's orders to provide counsel effectively forced them to violate these limits. The King County Executive argued it was prohibited by charter from providing counsel, as DPD has exclusive authority.
defendant_argument: Fairfax Hospital argued that caseload limits are merely guidelines and that the trial court has inherent authority to order DPD to provide counsel regardless of caseload limits.
decision_outcome: The court held that caseload limits in the Standards for Indigent Defense are mandatory and courts cannot order defense attorneys to violate them. It reversed the trial court's orders requiring the King County Executive to provide counsel, affirming DPD's exclusive authority. However, it affirmed the trial court's orders requiring DPD to provide counsel, finding that the trial court did not explicitly or implicitly order DPD to violate caseload limits.

title: State v. A.M.W.
description: Whether a court rule (JuCR 7.16) setting stricter prerequisites for juvenile arrest warrants conflicts with a state statute (RCW 13.40.040) and, if so, which provision prevails, with the plaintiff arguing the rule should prevail as procedural law and the defendant arguing the rule is substantive and outside the court's rule-making power.
plaintiff_argument: A.M.W. argued that JuCR 7.16 irreconcilably conflicts with RCW 13.40.040 and that JuCR 7.16 should trump the statute because it concerns procedural law, which is within the court's power to adopt.
defendant_argument: The State argued that JuCR 7.16, despite concerning warrant issuance procedure, acts as a substantive rule by limiting the State's ability to enforce the Juvenile Justice Act, and therefore falls outside the court's rule-making power.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals, holding that JuCR 7.16 is a procedural rule within the court's authority and can be harmonized with RCW 13.40.040 by requiring trial courts to apply both sets of prerequisites before issuing a juvenile arrest warrant.

title: Eyman v. Hobbs
description: Whether the Secretary of State has a mandatory duty to process a referendum on legislation that includes an emergency clause, and whether the emergency clause itself is valid.
plaintiff_argument: Eyman argues that the Secretary's inaction violated his constitutional right to file a referendum, contending that the Secretary has no discretion to refuse a properly filed referendum and that the emergency clause in ESHB 1296, § 603 is invalid because the legislature did not provide sufficient justification for its necessity.
defendant_argument: The Secretary refused to file the referendum on the basis that section 501 is subject to the emergency clause in ESHB 1296, § 603, and is therefore beyond the scope of the referendum power, arguing that as an executive branch officer, he lacks authority to override the legislature's declaration of emergency.
decision_outcome: The court denied Eyman's petition for a writ of mandamus, ruling that the Secretary of State had no mandatory duty to process the referendum because the legislation contained a valid emergency clause, making it exempt from referendum.

title: State v. Sabra Danielson, State v. Simone Nelson
description: Whether individuals with invalidated convictions have a right to be reimbursed for all court-imposed financial obligations, including labor performed in community service work, with the plaintiffs arguing for reimbursement based on equal protection and the defendants arguing against it, stating no such right exists.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs, Sabra K. Danielson and Simone Renee Nelson, argued that denying reimbursement for community service work, after their convictions were invalidated, violated their constitutional right to equal protection, as they were treated differently from wealthier individuals who paid LFOs in cash and were reimbursed.
defendant_argument: The defendant, State of Washington, argued that there is no established right to reimbursement for labor performed as community service in lieu of financial obligations, and therefore, the denial of such reimbursement did not violate equal protection.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, ruling that the petitioners did not demonstrate a right to be reimbursed for labor performed as community service in lieu of legal financial obligations, and thus, their equal protection claim failed.

title: State v. James Ellis
description: Whether the resentencing judge abused discretion by failing to consider Ellis's youthfulness and whether the restitution amount Ellis was ordered to pay violates the excessive fines clause of the state and federal constitutions.
plaintiff_argument: The resentencing judge abused discretion by failing to meaningfully consider his youthfulness, and the restitution amount imposed was excessive, violating the excessive fines clause.
defendant_argument: The resentencing judge did not abuse discretion, any error was harmless because Ellis received the sentence his counsel requested, and the restitution amount was not constitutionally excessive.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals regarding the resentencing judge's failure to consider Ellis's youth, remanding for a new sentencing hearing, but affirmed that the restitution amount was not excessive.

title: State v. Evans
description: Whether King County's administrative booking process, which involves patting down, handcuffing, and detaining out-of-custody pretrial defendants to collect fingerprints and identifying information, violates article I, section 7 of the Washington Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that the administrative booking process is authorized by law, citing exceptions to warrant requirements, RCW 10.98.050, and the Olsen balancing test. They contend that pretrial releasees have diminished privacy rights similar to detainees because they could have been arrested, and that the process is necessary for security and chain-of-custody.
defendant_argument: Kyle Evans argues that King County's administrative booking process, which includes pat-downs, handcuffing, and detention in a jail facility, constitutes an intrusion on his private affairs without authority of law, violating Article I, Section 7 of the Washington Constitution. He asserts that pretrial releasees do not have diminished privacy rights simply because they have been accused of a crime.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's order, ruling that King County's administrative booking process violates article I, section 7 of the Washington Constitution.

title: City of Wenatchee v. Stearns
description: Whether a police officer had reasonable suspicion to conduct a traffic stop for DUI based on a 911 tip, where the plaintiff argues the tip was reliable and corroborated by officer observations, and the defendant argues the tip was unreliable and uncorroborated.
plaintiff_argument: The 911 tip from a citizen eyewitness was reliable because it was contemporaneous and made to an emergency line, and it was sufficiently corroborated by the officer's observations of erratic driving, thus providing reasonable suspicion for the DUI stop.
defendant_argument: The traffic stop was unlawful for lack of reasonable suspicion because the 911 caller's tip was unreliable, not sufficiently corroborated by the officer's observations, and therefore did not justify the stop.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision and reinstated Frank Edward Stearns's convictions, finding the traffic stop was lawful.

title: State v. Mercedes
description: Whether Ferrier warnings, which advise individuals of their right to refuse, limit, and revoke consent to a warrantless search, are required when law enforcement seeks consent to search private property outside of a person's home.
plaintiff_argument: Ms. Mercedes argued that Ferrier warnings should apply to constitutionally recognized private affairs beyond the home, including her gated, fenced property, and that the officers' actions triggered these requirements.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Ferrier warnings are limited to searches of a person's home for contraband or evidence of a crime, and thus were not required for investigative visits to Ms. Mercedes's outdoor property.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals, concluding that Ferrier warnings were not required for the search of Ms. Mercedes's outdoor property, and remanded the case to determine if consent was voluntary under the totality of circumstances.

title: State v. Nelson
description: Whether community custody conditions requiring breath analysis (BA) and urinalysis (UA) testing to monitor compliance with alcohol and drug prohibitions are constitutionally permitted under Article I, Section 7 of the Washington Constitution, even if the underlying offenses are not crime-related to drug or alcohol use.
plaintiff_argument: Nelson argued that BA and UA testing conditions violate his constitutional right to privacy because his underlying offenses had no direct nexus to drug or alcohol use, making the testing an impermissible intrusion.
defendant_argument: The State argued that BA and UA testing conditions are constitutionally permitted and narrowly tailored to monitor compliance with validly imposed community custody conditions prohibiting alcohol and drug use, regardless of whether the underlying offenses were crime-related to drug or alcohol use.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that Nelson's preenforcement challenge was not ripe for review, but also affirmed that the BA and UA testing conditions are constitutional as they are narrowly tailored to monitor compliance with valid community custody conditions, regardless of the underlying offense's connection to drugs or alcohol.

title: State of Washington v. Gator's Custom Guns
description: Whether Engrossed Substitute Senate Bill 5078 (ESSB 5078), which bans the manufacture, distribution, importation, and sale of firearm magazines with a capacity of more than 10 rounds, violates the right to bear arms under the Washington and United States Constitutions.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that ESSB 5078 violates the right to bear arms because large capacity magazines are "arms" in common use for self-defense and are integral components for semi-automatic firearms to function as intended.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that ESSB 5078 is constitutional because large capacity magazines are not "arms" and are not commonly used for self-defense, nor is the right to purchase them an ancillary right necessary for self-defense.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the superior court's decision, ruling that ESSB 5078 is constitutional and does not violate the right to bear arms under either the Washington or United States Constitutions.

title: Vet Voice Foundation v. Hobbs
description: Whether signature verification in Washington's vote-by-mail system, which results in some lawfully cast ballots not being counted, facially violates the due process, privileges and immunities, and freedom of elections clauses of the state constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs contend that signature verification, because it results in some lawfully cast ballots not being counted, facially violates the due process, privileges and immunities, and freedom of elections clauses of the state constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that signature verification is a constitutional and integral part of the election system, essential for verifying voter identity and preventing fraud, especially when coupled with the expansive cure system in place.
decision_outcome: The court held that Washington's signature verification law, when coupled with the cure system, does not facially violate the state constitution's freedom of elections, privileges and immunities, or due process clauses, and granted summary judgment in favor of the defendants.

title: State v. McGee
description: Whether the state's attenuation doctrine allows police to apply for a warrant using tainted evidence when a new, independent criminal act lends new significance to the knowledge gained from that evidence, with the plaintiff arguing against such use and the defendant arguing for it.
plaintiff_argument: McGee argued that the July 13 warrant relied on evidence that should have been suppressed as fruit of the poisonous tree and that the trial court misapplied the state's attenuation doctrine, as the warrant application failed to establish probable cause without the illegally obtained evidence.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the attenuation doctrine allows police to use tainted evidence in a warrant application when a new, independent criminal act provides a new reason for its use, and that the superseding event only needs to occur between the unlawful police conduct and the prosecution's use of the tainted information.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals order, vacating McGee's conviction and remanding the case for a new trial, ruling that the attenuation doctrine does not allow for the use of illegally obtained evidence based on a new reason for its use.

title: State of Washington v. Luthi
description: Whether a criminal defendant may be required to appear for nonjury proceedings from an "in-court holding cell" without an individualized inquiry justifying such a restraint, with the plaintiff arguing against such a requirement and the defendant arguing it is permissible.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Cassandra Luthi, argued that requiring her to appear from an in-court holding cell without an individualized inquiry violated her due process rights, undermined the presumption of innocence, interfered with her ability to communicate with counsel, and violated the dignity of the proceedings.
defendant_argument: The defendant, State of Washington, argued that the in-court holding cell does not implicate due process rights, especially in nonjury hearings, and that any error was harmless because there was no jury and the courtroom was already in a jail.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the superior court's decision, holding that an individualized inquiry is required before a defendant can be compelled to appear from an in-court holding cell, and remanded for a new hearing.

title: Associated General Contractors of Washington v. State
description: Whether RCW 39.12.015(3), which requires the State to use collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) to set prevailing wage rates, violates Article II, Section 37 of the Washington Constitution by conflicting with RCW 39.12.026(1)'s single-county geographic limitation.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Associated General Contractors (AGC), argued that the newer law (RCW 39.12.015(3)) conflicts with the older statute (RCW 39.12.026(1)) because the single-county limitation applies to all data collected, including CBA data, thus violating Article II, Section 37.
defendant_argument: The defendant, State of Washington, argued that the single-county limitation in RCW 39.12.026(1) applies only to wage survey data collection, not to the newer CBA-adoption method, meaning no conflict exists and no constitutional violation.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals, holding that the newer statute (RCW 39.12.015(3)) does not violate Article II, Section 37 of the Washington Constitution because the older statute's single-county limitation (RCW 39.12.026(1)) applies only to wage survey data, not CBA-adopted wage rates.

title: Spokane County v. Meneses
description: Whether the Secretary of the Washington State Department of Social and Health Services (DSHS) is a 'state officer' for the purpose of the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction in mandamus, with the Prosecutor arguing yes and DSHS arguing no.
plaintiff_argument: The Prosecutor argued that the Secretary of DSHS is a 'state officer' under the Washington Constitution, allowing the court to exercise original jurisdiction and issue a writ of mandamus to compel DSHS to provide timely competency services.
defendant_argument: The Secretary of DSHS argued that the Secretary is not a 'state officer' within the meaning of the state constitution, therefore the court lacks original jurisdiction and must dismiss the petition.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed the petition for a writ of mandamus, concluding that the Secretary of DSHS is not a 'state officer' under article IV, section 4 of the Washington Constitution.

title: King County v. Abernathy
description: Whether a right-of-way approved by the United States Department of the Interior under the General Railroad Right-of-Way Act of 1875 constitutes a conveyance "patented by the United States" under Article XVII, Section 2 of the Washington State Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: King County argued that the right-of-way was "patented" land, meaning it never belonged to the State of Washington and therefore now belongs to King County.
defendant_argument: The Abernathys argued that the right-of-way was not "patented" land, meaning it belonged to Washington at statehood and is now owned by the homeowners.
decision_outcome: The court held that the right-of-way was an easement and not a land conveyance "patented by the United States" under the state constitution, thus the land belonged to Washington at statehood and is now owned by the homeowners.

title: Bennett v. United States
description: Whether Washington's eight-year statute of repose for medical malpractice actions violates the privileges and immunities clause of the Washington State Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing it is unconstitutional and the defendant arguing it is constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The eight-year statute of repose for medical malpractice actions violates the Washington Constitution's privileges and immunities clause by limiting the fundamental right to pursue common law claims.
defendant_argument: The eight-year statute of repose is constitutional, serves legitimate legislative purposes such as controlling malpractice insurance costs and barring stale claims, and therefore bars the plaintiff's claim.
decision_outcome: The court held that Washington's eight-year statute of repose for medical malpractice actions violates the privileges and immunities clause of article I, section 12 of the Washington State Constitution.

title: Gonzales v. Inslee
description: Whether Governor Inslee's COVID-19 eviction moratorium was lawful and within his statutory and constitutional authority.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the governor exceeded his statutory and constitutional authority by imposing the eviction moratorium, which unconstitutionally delegated legislative powers, impaired contracts, constituted a taking, violated access to courts, and violated separation of powers.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the eviction moratorium was lawful, within the governor's statutory authority, did not substantially impair contracts, did not constitute a taking, did not violate access to courts, and did not violate separation of powers.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower courts' decision, ruling that the governor's eviction moratorium was lawful and within his statutory and constitutional authority.

title: State v. Reynolds
description: Whether counting an adult conviction for a crime committed as a juvenile as a "strike" for a mandatory life without parole sentence violates state and federal constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment, with the plaintiff arguing it does and the defendant arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: Reynolds argues that imposing a sentence of life without parole (LWOP) based in part on his prior conviction for a crime committed as a juvenile violates state and federal constitutional protections against cruel or cruel and unusual punishments, citing the diminished culpability of juveniles.
defendant_argument: The State argues that Reynolds' current LWOP sentence punishes his current adult crime, not his prior juvenile offense, and that the "three strikes" law as applied to adults does not violate article I, section 14 of the Washington Constitution.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, upholding Michael Scott Reynolds, Jr.'s mandatory life in prison without possibility of parole sentence.

title: Snaza v. State
description: Whether RCW 10.116.030(3)(a), which requires county sheriffs to obtain authorization from the chair of the board of county commissioners before deploying tear gas to quell a riot, is unconstitutional because it interferes with the sheriff's core functions, with the plaintiffs arguing it is unconstitutional and the defendant arguing it is a valid legislative limitation.
plaintiff_argument: The Sheriffs argued that RCW 10.116.030(3)(a) is unconstitutional as it violates the constitutional separation of powers doctrine by interfering with the sheriff's core function of quelling riots, specifically by usurping the sheriff's discretionary authority to decide the manner in which a riot should be quelled.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the tear gas statute does not interfere with a core function of riot suppression, but rather imposes a valid limitation on the sheriff's discretion regarding the type of force used, and that such an intrusion is not extreme enough to violate Article XI, Section 5.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, holding that RCW 10.116.030(3)(a) is unconstitutional because it interferes with the sheriff's core functions, violating Article XI, Section 5 of the Washington Constitution.

title: Wahkiakum School District No. 200 v. State
description: Whether the "education" that the State has a paramount constitutional duty to amply fund includes school capital construction costs.
plaintiff_argument: The Wahkiakum School District (WSD) argued that the State is violating Article IX, Section 1 by failing to provide ample funds for school-related capital construction costs, asserting the State bears sole responsibility for such funding.
defendant_argument: The State of Washington argued that funding for school construction and other capital expenditures is governed by different constitutional provisions that primarily look to local school districts for funding assistance, indicating a shared responsibility.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision to dismiss the case, holding that the constitution does not include school capital construction costs within the category of "education" costs for which the State alone must make "ample provision."

title: State v. Teulilo
description: Whether Washington State's community caretaking exception to warrantless searches of homes is still valid after the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Caniglia v. Strom, with the petitioner arguing it is invalid and the respondent arguing it remains valid.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioner argued that the United States Supreme Court's decision in Caniglia v. Strom invalidates Washington State's community caretaking exception to the warrant requirement as applied to the home, making state cases recognizing a health and safety check exception invalid.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the community caretaking exception, including the health and safety check exception, remains intact post-Caniglia, and exigent circumstances still provide a valid exception to the warrant requirement.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision to deny the motion to suppress evidence, ruling that the warrantless entry was justified under the community caretaking exception.

title: State v. Rivers
description: Whether article I, section 21 and/or section 22 of the Washington State Constitution provide greater protection of the right to a jury venire drawn from a fair cross section of the community than the Sixth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Rivers argued that his fair cross section rights were violated due to the underrepresentation of Black jurors in King County's jury selection system, proposing a new test under state law or the elimination of the systematic exclusion requirement of the Duren test.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Rivers failed to demonstrate a violation of his fair cross section rights under existing federal or state constitutional frameworks, and that the King County jury assignment areas were created to promote jury participation and diversity.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Rivers's convictions, declining to adopt his proposed state constitutional tests for fair cross section claims and finding no systematic exclusion under the existing Duren test, but remanded for resentencing due to recent legislative changes.

title: Portugal v. Franklin County
description: Whether the Washington Voting Rights Act (WVRA) is facially valid and constitutional, with the plaintiff arguing it protects all voters from discrimination and the defendant arguing it is unconstitutional by favoring some racial groups.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Franklin County's electoral system violated the WVRA by diluting Latino/a votes, and that the WVRA itself is valid and protects all Washington voters from discrimination based on race, color, or language minority group.
defendant_argument: Gimenez argued that the WVRA is facially invalid and unconstitutional because it protects some racial groups while excluding others, thereby requiring local governments to implement electoral systems that favor some racial groups and disfavor others, and that the plaintiffs lacked standing.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, ruling that the WVRA is valid and constitutional on its face, protects all Washington voters from discrimination, and that the plaintiffs have standing. The court also awarded attorney fees and costs to the plaintiffs against Gimenez.

title: State v. Gonzalez (In re Sargent)
description: Whether "offenses punishable by the possibility of life in prison" under article I, section 20 of the Washington Constitution refers to the statutory maximum of the charged crime in general or the specific sentence the defendant is facing as charged.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that bail cannot be denied because the phrase "offenses punishable by the possibility of life in prison" refers to the specific sentence the defendant is facing as charged, which in their cases is less than life imprisonment under the SRA guidelines.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that the phrase "offenses punishable by the possibility of life in prison" refers to the statutory maximum of the offense in general, not the specific sentence the defendant is facing, and all Class A felonies carry a statutory maximum of life in prison.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower courts' decisions, ruling that bail can be denied for defendants charged with Class A felonies because such offenses are punishable by the possibility of life in prison, regardless of the specific sentence the defendant is facing.

title: Quinn v. State
description: Whether the Washington capital gains tax is a property tax subject to constitutional uniformity and levy limitations, or a valid excise tax, and whether it violates the state's privileges and immunities clause or the federal dormant commerce clause.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the capital gains tax is a property tax on income, violating Article VII's uniformity and levy limitations, and also violates the privileges and immunities clause of the Washington Constitution and the federal dormant commerce clause.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the capital gains tax is a valid excise tax, not a property tax, and is consistent with all state and federal constitutional requirements.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the superior court's grant of summary judgment to the plaintiffs, holding that the capital gains tax is a valid excise tax and is consistent with the state and federal constitutions, and remanded for further proceedings.

title: Hanson v. Carmona
description: Whether RCW 4.96.020(4), a presuit claims notice statute, applies when a plaintiff sues a governmental employee acting in the scope of her employment in her individual capacity, and whether this statute violates separation of powers because it conflicts with CR 3(a).
plaintiff_argument: Hanson argued that the presuit notice requirement does not apply to an employee sued in their individual capacity, as such a case is not against the sovereign state, and that the statute violates separation of powers by conflicting with court rules for commencing a lawsuit.
defendant_argument: Carmona argued that the presuit notice requirement applies because she was acting within the scope of employment, and the government entity would be bound by any judgment, and that the indemnity statute means she cannot be held personally liable.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals, holding that RCW 4.96.020(4) applies to government employees acting within the scope of employment even when sued individually, and that the statute does not violate separation of powers, remanding for summary judgment in favor of Carmona.

title: State v. Meredith
description: Whether the method of fare enforcement, involving armed and uniformed police officers on a moving bus, constituted an unlawful seizure and disturbed a transit passenger's private affairs under Article I, Section 7 of the Washington Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The method of fare enforcement used by armed, uniformed police officers on a moving bus constituted an unlawful seizure and violated his right to privacy.
defendant_argument: The fare enforcement was lawful, either because the passenger consented by boarding the bus or under a "special needs doctrine," and did not constitute an unlawful seizure.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, ruling that Meredith was unlawfully seized and remanded the case to the trial court for further proceedings.

title: Washington Food Industry Association v. City of Seattle
description: Whether the City of Seattle's ordinance requiring hazard pay for gig workers and imposing other constraints on food delivery network companies is valid under state statutory and constitutional law.
plaintiff_argument: Instacart argues the ordinance is invalid because it imposes an illegal tax on groceries, exceeds police powers, constitutes a regulatory taking, impairs contracts, and violates equal protection and privileges and immunities clauses.
defendant_argument: The City of Seattle argues the ordinance is a valid exercise of its police powers to protect gig workers and public health during the COVID-19 pandemic, and that the premium pay is not a tax.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed Instacart's claims challenging the ordinance based on the RCW 82.84 statute, equal protection, and privileges and immunities, but allowed Instacart's claims regarding regulatory takings, contracts clause, 42 U.S.C. § 1983 damages, and police powers to proceed to trial.

title: State v. Bagby
description: Whether a prosecutor's repeated use of racially coded language and differential treatment of witnesses based on race constituted flagrant prosecutorial misconduct that undermined the defendant's right to a fair trial.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecutor's use of race and the term "nationality" evoked racial bias, constituting prosecutorial misconduct that negatively impacted the trial and required reversal of convictions. The prosecutor intentionally used these tactics to appeal to racial biases against Black defendants.
defendant_argument: The prosecutor's use of "nationality" was incorrect but not an intentional appeal to racial bias, serving instead to help witnesses identify the defendant. Even if it were misconduct, the error would have been harmless given the substantial evidence.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, vacating the defendant's convictions and remanding the case to the trial court for a new trial.

title: Washington State Council of County & City Employees v. City of Spokane
description: Whether a municipal ordinance requiring all collective bargaining between the city and union representatives to be open to the public is preempted by state law and unconstitutional under the Washington State Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (Union) argued that the Spokane City Charter's section 40, which mandates open collective bargaining, is preempted by state law (PECBA) and unconstitutional because it conflicts with the state's uniform collective bargaining framework.
defendant_argument: The defendant (City of Spokane) argued that section 40 is not preempted by PECBA, as PECBA only regulates mandatory subjects of bargaining, leaving permissive subjects like negotiation procedures open for local regulation, and that the ordinance was not strictly mandatory.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's ruling, holding that section 40 of the Spokane City Charter is preempted by state law and is unconstitutional under article XI, section 11 of the Washington State Constitution.

title: Associated General Contractors of Washington v. State
description: Whether Substitute Senate Bill (SSB) 5493, which modifies how the Department of Labor and Industries calculates prevailing wage rates for public works projects, constitutes an unconstitutional delegation of legislative authority.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Associated General Contractors, argued that SSB 5493 is an unconstitutional delegation of legislative authority because it requires the industrial statistician to use wages from collective bargaining agreements (CBAs), effectively delegating legislative power to private parties.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the State of Washington, argued that SSB 5493 is constitutional because the legislature made a policy decision to adopt the highest CBA wage rate and delegated the authority to identify and adopt that rate to the industrial statistician, not to private parties, and that adequate standards and procedural safeguards exist.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that SSB 5493 does not violate the nondelegation doctrine and is constitutional.

title: State v. Anderson
description: Whether Tonelli Anderson's 61-year sentence for crimes committed as a juvenile is unconstitutionally cruel under Washington's constitution, with the plaintiff arguing it is unconstitutional based on a bright-line rule from State v. Haag, and the defendant arguing it is constitutional because Haag does not establish such a bright-line rule for all juvenile offenders.
plaintiff_argument: Anderson argued his 61-year sentence is unconstitutionally cruel because State v. Haag established a bright-line rule prohibiting juvenile sentences of 46 years or longer.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Anderson's interpretation of Haag is incorrect and that Haag does not create a bright-line rule for all juvenile offenders, especially when crimes do not reflect mitigating qualities of youth.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Tonelli Anderson's 61-year sentence, ruling it is constitutionally permissible under Washington's Article I, Section 14.

title: State v. Sum
description: Whether the race and ethnicity of an allegedly seized person are relevant circumstances in determining when a warrantless seizure occurred under Article I, Section 7 of the Washington Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Sum argued that he was unlawfully seized without reasonable suspicion and that his race and ethnicity should be considered as relevant circumstances in the seizure analysis.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Sum was not seized until he drove off at high speed, and that Sum's race was not relevant in this specific case without evidence of discrimination or influence on the deputy's actions.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals, holding that Sum was unlawfully seized before providing a false name and birth date, and formally recognized that race and ethnicity are relevant in law enforcement interactions for seizure analysis.

title: Bass v. City of Edmonds
description: Whether a city ordinance requiring guns to be stored safely and kept out of unauthorized hands is preempted by state law.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the city ordinance requiring safe firearm storage and preventing unauthorized access is preempted by state law (RCW 9.41.290).
defendant_argument: The City of Edmonds argued that the state preemption statute (RCW 9.41.290) only preempts regulation in specific enumerated areas or that storage regulations are not preempted under the principle of ejusdem generis.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that the city ordinance requiring safe firearm storage is preempted by state law.

title: Kellogg v. National Railroad Passenger Corp.
description: Whether the 2019 amendments to Washington's wrongful death statute apply retroactively to allow new beneficiaries to assert claims despite a prior settlement, and if this retroactive application violates the state constitution's due process or contracts clauses.
plaintiff_argument: The 2019 amendments should apply retroactively to allow James' siblings to bring wrongful death claims, as the prior settlement only covered existing beneficiaries and did not waive future claims.
defendant_argument: The 2019 amendments should not apply retroactively because it would violate Amtrak's contracts clause and due process rights, as the prior settlement released all claims related to James' death.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed that the 2019 amendments apply retroactively, allowing new beneficiaries to assert wrongful death claims, and that this does not violate the state constitution's due process or contracts clauses.

title: State v. Elwell
description: Whether the open view doctrine applies to justify a warrantless search of a covered object, and whether Daniel Ethan Elwell was deprived of his right to counsel when his attorney disagreed with bringing a motion to suppress.
plaintiff_argument: Elwell argued that the officer conducted an unlawful search by removing the blanket and plastic wrapping from the object, as its identity was not immediately apparent, and that he was deprived of his right to counsel when forced to proceed pro se on his motion to suppress.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the open view doctrine applied because Elwell and the covered object were immediately recognizable from surveillance footage, justifying the officer's actions, and that Elwell was not deprived of counsel as his attorney provided assistance.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Elwell's conviction, holding that while the officer's actions constituted an unlawful, warrantless search in violation of the Washington Constitution, the error was harmless, and Elwell was not deprived of his right to counsel.

title: State v. Bowman
description: Whether law enforcement's use of information obtained from a consensual search of a third party's cell phone to set up a separate text message exchange with the defendant, posing as the third party, violated the defendant's privacy rights under state and federal constitutions.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the consensual search of the third party's phone provided the necessary authority of law, and the subsequent police ruse using lawfully obtained information did not constitute a privacy invasion or trespass.
defendant_argument: Bowman argued that both the search of the third party's phone and the subsequent police ruse violated his privacy rights under state and federal constitutions, and that the text messages constituted an unconstitutional trespass.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision and reinstated Bowman's conviction, holding that law enforcement's actions did not violate Bowman's privacy rights or constitute a trespass.

title: Wash. State Legislature v. Inslee
description: Whether Governor Inslee exceeded his constitutional veto authority by striking a "fuel type condition" from an appropriations bill, with the Legislature arguing the condition was not a complete appropriation item and thus not subject to veto, and the Governor arguing it was a complete appropriation item or violated other constitutional articles.
plaintiff_argument: The Washington State Legislature argued that the fuel type condition did not constitute a complete appropriation item and was therefore not subject to gubernatorial veto, and that it complied with constitutional articles II, sections 19 and 37.
defendant_argument: Governor Inslee argued that the fuel type condition constituted a complete appropriation item subject to gubernatorial veto, or alternatively, that it violated Article II, sections 19 and 37.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's summary judgment, ruling that Governor Inslee exceeded his constitutional veto power by striking the fuel type condition, which was a valid legislative limit on executive agency expenditure and not substantive law.

title: State v. Peterson
description: Whether RCW 69.50.410, a statute criminalizing the sale of drugs, is invalid and unconstitutional due to implied repeal, desuetude, or violation of the state constitution's privileges and immunities clause, and whether its sentencing provisions conflict with the Sentencing Reform Act (SRA).
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that RCW 69.50.410 is valid and constitutional, and that its sentencing provisions can be harmonized with the Sentencing Reform Act (SRA).
defendant_argument: Peterson argues that RCW 69.50.410 is invalid and unconstitutional due to implied repeal, desuetude, and violation of the state constitution's privileges and immunities clause, and that its sentencing provisions cannot be reconciled with the SRA.
decision_outcome: The court rejected Peterson's arguments, finding RCW 69.50.410 valid and constitutional, and remanded the case for resentencing under the Sentencing Reform Act (SRA).

title: In re Williams
description: Whether the conditions of Robert Rufus Williams's confinement constituted cruel punishment under article I, section 14 of the Washington State Constitution, with Williams arguing they were cruel due to lack of basic necessities and assistance for his disabilities, and the Department of Corrections arguing they were not and had taken steps to mitigate risks.
plaintiff_argument: Williams argued that his conditions of confinement, including lack of reasonable access to bathroom facilities, running water, and appropriate assistance for his disabilities, constituted cruel punishment under state and federal constitutions, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic, and sought release to home confinement.
defendant_argument: The Department of Corrections (DOC) denied Williams's request for extraordinary medical placement, stating he failed to satisfy community safety criteria. DOC also contended that Williams's violent offense and continued risk to the community justified his confinement, and that they had taken numerous steps to stem the spread of COVID-19.
decision_outcome: The court granted Williams's personal restraint petition, concluding that his conditions of confinement constituted cruel punishment under article I, section 14 of the Washington State Constitution, and directed DOC to remedy these conditions or release Williams.

title: In re Monschke
description: Whether the constitutional requirement for judicial discretion in sentencing, which forbids mandatory life without parole (LWOP) for those under 18, also forbids such sentences for 18- to 21-year-old defendants.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argue that mandatory LWOP sentences are unconstitutionally cruel when applied to youthful defendants aged 18-21, as modern neuroscience shows no clear line between childhood and adulthood, and these individuals share similar mitigating qualities of youth as juveniles, requiring individualized sentencing.
defendant_argument: The State argues that the legislature's age of majority (18) is not arbitrary and that individuals aged 18 and older are adults who should be held fully accountable and face the full legal consequences of their actions, without requiring individualized sentencing based on brain development.
decision_outcome: The court granted the personal restraint petitions, vacating the mandatory life without parole sentences for the 19- and 20-year-old defendants, and remanded their cases for new sentencing hearings where the trial court must consider the mitigating qualities of youth.

title: State v. Blake
description: Whether Washington's strict liability drug possession statute, RCW 69.50.4013, which punishes innocent and passive conduct without proof of intent, exceeds the legislature's police power and violates due process.
plaintiff_argument: Blake argued that the strict liability drug possession statute, which penalizes conduct without requiring the State to prove a guilty mind, exceeds the legislature's police power and violates due process, and that requiring her to prove unwitting possession also violates due process.
defendant_argument: The State contended that the statute is a valid exercise of police power, that the judicially created affirmative defense of "unwitting possession" saves the statute from unconstitutionality, and that declaring it unconstitutional would undermine other strict liability crimes.
decision_outcome: The Washington Supreme Court ruled that RCW 69.50.4013, the strict liability drug possession statute, violates the due process clauses of the state and federal constitutions by criminalizing wholly innocent and passive nonconduct, and therefore vacated Blake's conviction.

title: Woods v. Seattle's Union Gospel Mission
description: Whether the religious employer exemption in Washington's Law Against Discrimination (WLAD) is constitutional as applied to an employee whose job duties are not ministerial, given the employee's fundamental rights to sexual orientation and marriage, or if it allows religious nonprofits to discriminate without reasonable grounds.
plaintiff_argument: Matthew Woods argued that the religious employer exemption in WLAD is unconstitutional as applied to him because his staff attorney job duties were unrelated to religious practices, and it violates his fundamental rights to sexual orientation and marriage.
defendant_argument: Seattle's Union Gospel Mission (SUGM) argued that the religious employer exemption applies to its hiring decisions because all its employees are expected to minister to clients, and holding it liable under WLAD would violate its free exercise rights.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the summary judgment granted to SUGM and remanded the case to the trial court to determine whether SUGM's staff attorneys qualify as ministers under the ministerial exception, which would then determine if the religious employer exemption applies to Matthew Woods.
